newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Slim spending, exports may cut US Q3 GDP.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Slim spending, exports may cut US Q3 GDP.

text.p: Sharp declines in personal consumption, exports and government spending should slash the third-quarter U.S. growth rate by more than half from the spring's heady pace, analysts said.

"There are lots and lots of reasons for the slowdown in the third quarter and those are consumption, exports and particularly government spending," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
He said consumption should post a significant drop from the 3.4 percent pace registered in Q2 to about 1.7 percent.

Economists in a Reuters survey forecast third quarter Gross Domestic Product rose at a 1.8 percent annual rate, down from 4.7 percent second quarter growth. Forecasts ranged from 0.8 percent to 2.5 percent.
The data are slated for release via the U.S. Commerce Department at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Wednesday, October 30.
John Williams, chief global markets economist at BT Securities Corp, also pointed to waning consumption data through the summer in his forecast for 1.8-percent GDP.
"We have solid evidence that the consumer slowed spending sharply in the third quarter, so final sales are probably going to be at 1.0 percent or less," Williams said.

Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said final sales should be either flat or up 0.2 percent. That number should pick up into the fourth quarter, she said.
Despite the clear weakness in third quarter consumer spending, Williams said blips in forecasts may occur as a result of experts underestimating consumer strength.
In fact, he said the third-quarter slowdown is likely to be temporary and predicts a fourth quarter rebound will put the Federal Reserve back on a bent to tigthen monetary policy.
"There's strong job income growth, high confidence given the low unemployment rate and the consumer is ready to go on spending in a big way here," Williams said.

Declines in exports since the second quarter also represented a challenge to third quarter economic growth, economists said. The growth rate of exports declined from 5.7 percent in Q2 to 3.5 percent in Q3, Johnson said, a drop that was not matched by a decline in the growth rate of imports.
Government spending, which took the markets by surprise in the second quarter with a 9.4 percent rise, could be the GDP component with the biggest reversal, economists said.
The statistic should come in at -6.0 to -7.0 percent in the third quarter, Johnson said.
Furthermore, Schaja tacked flat housing and construction data into the recipe for slower Q3 GDP.
Schaja noted any surprise in the report may stem from inventory rebuilding in the third quarter. She added it is difficult to know how the government collects and measures such data.
"Consumption we know based on figures for July and August, so that won't be as big of a surprise," she said.
Inventory rebuilding "is why the final sales number is so much lower than the overall number, so (inventories) are a little bit of a question mark going into (GDP)," Schaja said.
Schaja also said business investments may also take the markets by surprise with a stronger-than-expected read.

Johnson said moderate non-inflationary growth will continue into the fourth quarter and 1997. Williams said GDP will reaccelerate in the fourth quarter, however, based on his outlook of higher job growth and consumer confidence.
DLJ's Schaja expects a slightly stronger 1.5 percent to 2.0 percent rate of growth in the fourth quarter (from the Q3 forecast of 1.4 percent) based on her expectations of stronger final sales.
